analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces Medicaid and Medicare Part A with block grants and private-insurance subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bill had one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and died in House committees without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act and its coverage expansions, then rebuild health policy around private insurance and tax-favored savings accounts. It would end the Medicaid and CHIP entitlements and replace them with fixed block grants to states capped at 25% of what the federal government spent on those programs in 2012. It would also replace the Medicare Part A hospital entitlement with a subsidy for buying private insurance, let insurers sell plans governed by whichever state's rules they choose, and greatly expand health savings accounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income taxpayers who use health savings accounts (the contribution cap would rise to $10,000, no high-deductible plan required, and no penalty on non-medical withdrawals); health insurers, which could sell plans governed by the least-regulated state they pick and would receive premium-subsidy payments from the new Medicare program; and physicians, who would get a tax credit of up to $8,000 for charity care.

how_it_helps.text: Health savings accounts would become far more generous: the contribution deduction would rise to $10,000 per person ($20,000 for couples), the high-deductible-plan requirement would be dropped, Medicare-eligible people could contribute, and the penalty on distributions not used for medical expenses would be repealed [S2][S3].

The bill creates a Medicare Reform Premium Assistance Program that pays new seniors an amount equal to the median premium plus median deductible of individual-market insurance in their area, usable for private plans or medical savings accounts [S3].

Physicians providing at least 25 hours of charity care would receive a tax credit scaling up to $8,000 at 100 hours, and taxpayers would get a credit for gifts providing medical care to the indigent [S3].

Health insurers could designate one 'primary state' whose insurance laws would govern policies sold anywhere, exempting them from the other states' benefit mandates, rate rules, and most consumer-protection laws — the bill's own required notice tells buyers a policy 'may be less expensive... because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Low-income people who rely on Medicaid and CHIP, whose federal guarantee of coverage would end and be replaced by a block grant fixed at 25% of fiscal-year 2012 federal spending for those programs — a large cut — with states allowed to divert up to 30% of it to other welfare programs. People with pre-existing conditions would lose ACA protections when Title I is repealed and pre-2010 law is restored. Seniors would see Medicare Part A entitlement replaced by a private-insurance subsidy that may buy less coverage, and the agency that administers Medicare and Medicaid would be phased out into the Treasury Department.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid recipients, pre-existing-condition patients, and seniors

drawbacks.text: The Medicaid/CHIP block grant is set at 25% of fiscal-year 2012 federal spending for those programs and is not an entitlement for individuals, so coverage for the poor would depend on state budget choices and could be cut in a recession, with states allowed to shift up to 30% of the money to non-health programs like SNAP [S3].

Repealing Title I of the ACA and restoring the law as it stood before 2010 would remove its coverage expansions and protections, and the cross-state insurance provision would let insurers avoid most consumer-protection and benefit-requirement laws of the state where the buyer lives — the bill's mandatory disclosure warns purchasers of exactly that [S2][S3].

Replacing Medicare Part A entitlement with a premium subsidy and eliminating the CMS agency would convert a defined guaranteed benefit into a payment toward commercial insurance whose cost and coverage the government does not guarantee [S3].

The expanded HSA and medical-deduction provisions (no 10% floor, no 2% floor, no OTC-drug restriction) deliver their largest tax value to people with high incomes who can afford to set aside and itemize thousands of dollars [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains — bigger tax-advantaged accounts, cheaper less-regulated plans for healthy buyers, a small charity-care credit — are modest and skew toward people who are already well off. Its costs fall on people with the least: a block grant set at a quarter of prior-year federal Medicaid/CHIP spending, loss of ACA coverage protections, and conversion of Medicare's hospital entitlement into a subsidy for commercial insurance. The bill does include some consumer safeguards (an external-appeals process, a ban on re-rating sick individuals, a federal floor before an issuer can sell across state lines), but the overall design shifts risk from insurers and the federal government onto low-income and older patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced and never advanced, so it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun of Georgia introduced the bill on August 1, 2013, with introductory remarks in the House [S1][S5].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to eight committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, House Administration, Appropriations, and Rules — and days later to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs [S5].
No cosponsor ever signed on [S4], and no committee reported the bill or scheduled any markup or floor action [S5].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill lapsed without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Affordable Care Act's coverage protections, the Medicaid and CHIP entitlements, and traditional Medicare Part A all remained in place — so the people who depend on them are better off than they would have been under this law. Insurers also avoided the abrupt transition, keeping the ACA market they had adapted to rather than facing both repeal and deregulated cross-state competition at once.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People covered by the ACA, Medicaid, and Medicare

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and was never taken up by the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Repealing the ACA would have removed the individual mandate that created customers and the ACA's insurance rules, while the cross-state provision would let insurers sell plans governed by whichever state's laws they designate, escaping other states' benefit mandates and rate rules. The Medicare premium-assistance program would route public money to insurers as payments for private coverage. In this bill, insurers' flexibility comes directly at the cost of the coverage rules their customers live under.

industries.industry: High-income households with health savings accounts
industries.note: The bill raises HSA contribution limits to $10,000 ($20,000 joint), removes the high-deductible-plan requirement, allows Medicare-eligible people to contribute, repeals the penalty on non-medical withdrawals, and removes floors on medical-expense deductions. These are tax benefits that require money to set aside, so their value concentrates among higher earners while the underlying coverage protections are repealed.

Physicians would get a tax credit of $2,000 to $8,000 depending on charity-care hours, plus the removal of the over-the-counter drug restriction on tax-advantaged accounts. The credit is modest and rewards care doctors would otherwise donate, so the gain is small relative to the health-system changes elsewhere in the bill.

The EMTALA changes would let a broader range of staff perform initial triage and narrow the emergency-condition definition, potentially reducing uncompensated emergency care obligations. Meanwhile, replacing Medicare Part A with premium subsidies and shifting Medicaid to block grants would change who arrives at the hospital insured at all.
